summary: Describes a PPP Network Control Protocol for the LAN extension interface, used with an intelligent device that connects a remote site to the network. It defines control packets for startup and remote commands, including filtering. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A set of rules letting a small remote box act as a stretched-out part of the office network.

subtitle: Protocol for connecting remote LANs transparently over serial point-to-point links using PPP

tldr.problem: Remote offices and home workers need transparent LAN connectivity to a central office, but traditional routers are complex to configure and require technical expertise. Simple devices for non-network-literate users were needed.
tldr.mechanism: A LAN extension interface unit connects a remote LAN to a central router across a serial WAN link using PPP. The unit filters and bridges MAC frames, negotiates parameters with the router's virtual interface, and carries both data frames and remote control commands in-band over the same link.
tldr.outcome: Remote LANs appear as local interfaces to the central router, using standard routing without complex configuration, and remote managers can configure and monitor the device through control packets over the same link.

today: RFC 1841 is an Informational document describing a Cisco-specific technology from the mid-1990s. While the LAN extension concept remains relevant, modern remote connectivity uses VPN tunneling, broadband access, and cloud-hosted networks. The PPP-LEX protocol itself is not widely deployed beyond Cisco equipment of that era.

sections.title: Extending LANs Over Serial Links
sections.content:
More people work from home offices and remote branch offices, requiring Internet access but without the network expertise to run a router. A LAN extension interface unit is a simpler alternative: a hardware box installed at the remote site that bridges a LAN across a WAN link to a central router. The central router has a virtual interface for each remote unit, mirroring its characteristics. To routing protocols, the virtual interface looks like a local interface, keeping state (up or down), and identifying the remote unit by MAC address.

Unlike traditional bridging, LAN extension units depend entirely on the central router—they cannot operate standalone or back-to-back. They do not require spanning tree algorithms. They transfer MAC frames across the serial line like bridges do, but the central router decides whether to route or bridge the incoming traffic. The topology uses only one subnet per remote LAN instead of two (as router-to-router links do), because the virtual interface's IP address is in the same subnet as the remote LAN's nodes.
sections.eli5: The magic box sits at your remote site and connects your LAN to the main office router across a phone line. The main office router sees it as just another local network plugged in, even though it is miles away.

sections.title: Stack and Data Flow
sections.content:
The LAN extension interface architecture separates inbound and outbound directions. Inbound (remote LAN to router), the unit receives MAC frames from the local LAN, optionally filters them by protocol type or MAC address to optimize WAN bandwidth, passes survivors to the PPP state machine, adds PPP encapsulation, and sends the frame across the serial link. The router receives it, decapsulates the PPP header, and passes it to the virtual interface for normal routing or bridging.

Outbound (router to remote LAN), the router's virtual interface builds the full MAC header and adds PPP encapsulation before sending across the serial link. The remote unit strips the PPP header and forwards the frame directly onto the LAN, with no additional filtering—the router has already decided this frame goes to this unit. Control commands and statistics requests from the router are embedded in-band in a separate encapsulation (protocol type 0x8041) alongside the data packets (protocol type 0x0041), allowing remote configuration and management without a separate control channel.
sections.eli5: Data going out from the office gets wrapped in the protocol layer, sent across the line, and unwrapped at the box. Data from your office network gets wrapped, sent, and delivered to your LAN. Control commands ride along in special packets so the office can manage the box remotely.

sections.title: PPP-LEX: Negotiation and Control
sections.content:
PPP-LEX is a new Network Control Protocol (NCP) for PPP. The LAN extension interface unit and router first exchange standard PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP) packets to establish and configure the serial link. Once the link is open, they exchange PPP-LEX NCP packets to negotiate parameters.

The unit initiates by sending a startup options packet containing MAC type (e.g., Ethernet), MAC address, and LAN extension version. The router responds with Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, or Configure-Rej. Once acknowledged, the PPP-LEX NCP reaches an opened state, and both parties can exchange PPP-LEX data packets and remote command packets. The router initiates remote commands to control the unit and gather statistics. The unit responds with Ack (success), Nak (negotiation failure), or Rej (reject). Commands include setting filters, enabling/disabling the interface, requesting statistics, downloading firmware, and retrieving inventory information.
sections.eli5: When the box first connects, it tells the office what kind of LAN it is and what its address is. The office says okay and they start sending data. Any time the office wants to ask the box for status or change a setting, it sends a command and the box replies whether it worked.

sections.title: Filtering and Remote Commands
sections.content:
The LAN extension unit can filter inbound frames by protocol type or by source MAC address, helping conserve WAN bandwidth by blocking traffic that the office does not need. Filters are set via remote commands from the router.

Remote command options allow the router to configure and monitor the unit. Commands include Filter Protocol Type (block certain protocols), Filter MAC Address (block certain MAC addresses), Set Priority (traffic prioritization), Enable/Disable (turn the interface on or off), Reboot, Request Statistics (get packet and byte counts), Download Request/Data/Status (firmware updates), and Inventory Request (query hardware and software versions). Each command is encoded in a LAN Extension Interface Protocol packet with option types and flags, allowing the office to manage the device without requiring a technician to visit the site.
sections.eli5: The office can tell the box to ignore certain kinds of traffic to save bandwidth, to stop working temporarily, or to download new software. The office can also ask the box for statistics on how much data passed through or what hardware it has.

sections.title: Frame Structure
sections.content:
Both control and data packets follow a layered format. The outermost layer is the standard PPP header: Address field (always 0xFF, the all-stations address), Control field (always 0x03, unnumbered information), and Protocol Type (0x8041 for control, 0x0041 for data).

Inside, the LAN Extension Interface Protocol header contains a Code field (type of packet: Configure-Request, Ack, Nak, Rej), Identifier field (to match requests and responses), and Length field (total packet length).

For startup options, the payload contains Option-Type, Option-Length, and Option-Data for each option. For remote commands, the payload contains Option-Type and Option-Flags. For data packets, the payload is the encapsulated MAC frame with address and control information.
sections.eli5: Every packet has a PPP wrapper on the outside, then the type and length information, then the actual content—either control options, command flags, or the network frame being forwarded.
